blocks.x: Ready to go. First thing we usually ask is your name. Your full name.
Peter Edwin Boccage. Boccage in French, you know.
Boccage in English.
In English, yeah.
And when were you born and where?
July the 31st, 1887.
This side of the river or over there?
Algiers, right here in Algiers, yeah.
Exactly what bought Algiers.
Right up here, about two, three blocks up there on Brooklyn. And I think it was Ptolemy Street, you know. My grandfather at the time had a, when there was a farm, like, you know, truck farm.
I see. Speaking of your grandfather, did he play music?
No, no.
Anybody?

My father played. My father? Yeah, he played something he was living. In those days, he used to use four pieces, you know, a bass, violin, a guitar, and a violin, and a trumpet, and play a whole ball, you know. They didn't have no big bands like we have today, you know. He was a guitar player. He was a guitar player.
And do you remember any of the fellows he played with?
Well, yeah, they all did. No, there's the violinist. He was my first teacher. His name was De Fuentes. And the bass violin player was Jim Dorsey. And the trumpet player was Mineta. My Mineta's uncle.
Is that Norman?
Norman, yeah, yes. That's right. That was the four piece combination.
And your teacher, his full name, do you remember?
Henry De Fuentes.
Henry De Fuentes.
De Fuentes, yeah.
That sounds like Spanish.

That is, yes. He first taught me violin, you know. And then I had an, after he got through, I had a Frenchman from over in the city. He used to come over and give me lessons. When I was a kid, then I was around about in my teens then, you know, 14, 15, like that. When I got about, well, 17, I started to play professionally, you know. Playing in bands, dances, doing stuff. Nothing.
What was this teacher's name from across the river, the Frenchman?
Well, I know it was Ferdinand, but I can't think of his last name, you know. He was from France. I have a manuscript there that he wrote. I think his name is on it. I'll show it to you before you go.
Oh, I would like very much to see it. Now, you've got a fine collection of things. You showed me some of your pictures.

Mm-hmm. Quite a bit of pictures, yeah. Well, I played the violin, man, until about, about 1918 I started playing brass, you know. Mm-hmm. But all the former years I played nothing but the violin, you know.
That's all, until 1918?
Yeah, when I was with Bunk and them.
Had you ever played anything else, guitar, bass?

Well, I played, we played the St. Charles. We had a four-piece combination there, and I played the Banger Madeline, you know. And we had a violin, piano, drums, and mandolin, Piran, you know. Mm-hmm. And Cottrell was on drums, old man Cottrell, you know. Mm-hmm. And a fellow, he died in Chicago called him Frank Ahenia, a piano player. You might have saw him around Chicago.
No, I've heard of him.
Yeah, but he, he died of that. Well, we played our whole season, you know, in the Italian garden in St. Charles, you know.
What was Frankie Ahenia's last name exactly? How do you pronounce that? Ahenia?
Ahenia. That's what we used to call him, Frank Ahenia. I don't know how he spelled it, though.
I haven't done some music. Piran published some of his music.
Yes, uh-huh.
That would be right then, no doubt. Mm-hmm.
That's what we used to call him.
I see.
Who did you play your first job with?

Oh, I started playing with this, this combination with my dad and them, you know. And then we started playing over in the city, you see. Playing around, around the story of the early head, dance halls, you remember that. And we used to use, one time they cut out the brass, you see.
Mm-hmm.

And just use strings. So then I played back there a while, you know. And then eventually I started playing with the band, like Sapir Band, you know, and different bands like that, you know. And, and, and Piran, you know. And then finally I started playing brass. And then we stayed out the Spanish food for Tranchini out there ten years on that job, you know. Mm-hmm. And then big restaurant out at Spanish food out there. Well, that was the Piran band, see. Mm-hmm. We started with a string aggregation and we wound up with eight-piece orchestra. That's then we went to New York, you know, recorded for the Victor OK in the Columbia. Mm-hmm. We played the Rosalind Ballroom, eight-piece band, you know. That's the pictures I showed you. You remember that? No. And we came back and we went back out there again while we was away. Celestine was out there at Razorland. But when they came back, the people wanted us back, so we went back on that job again. And when he closed up out there, then we went up in Metry for old man Dominic Tranchini then at the Beverly Garden. We played there for him and then we went to the Victory Inn. I don't know if you remember. I think you might have been too young for that.
No, I don't remember.
But that Victory Inn was the time they had that great killing scrape there between the friends. He was gamblers, you know.
Mm-hmm.

He fell off on Broadway there. They got into Humbug somewhere. They were all friends but they wound up murdering one another, you know. Some were from St. Louis and some were from Detroit, you know. But they actually had a $100,000 bankroll in that house. Yes, indeed man. And we played there. We had a six-piece combination there. There was plenty of money in those days. We used to make $20, $30 a piece, just collection. And we were getting $60-some dollars a week salary, you know. All them guys, the money was like water with them, you know.
Mm-hmm. All that, the gambling.

And then over on Tranchini opened another place in Metro. It's a church now, a great big place there on the highway. They converted it into a church. And we stayed there a while. Then we went to Suburban Garden for Jack Sheen. We worked there a couple years. And it was all with Piron. Yeah, all with Piron, yeah. And finally, Louis came down at Suburban Garden. Well, we were to go back in there, but we had a kind of misunderstanding between old man Tranchini and Piron. We didn't go, so they sat and got Louis in the job. So that's when Louis came from Chicago and went into Suburban Garden.
I was wondering about when you, how did you tell how old you were when you started in music on violin, taking lessons?
Yes, I was about 12. About 12. About 12, yeah. About, oh, about four years I was gone. I was playing. Mm-hmm. I was, in fact, I was just fast, you know.
How did your father play and those fellows you played with, what style did they play?

Well, they played at old time. You see, those days they had music that mostly looked like manuscript, but they called it German music, you know. They used to come from the old country, you know. Mm-hmm. And that's what they played. And they had a set of books they called Manhattan books, dance books, you know. Well, they had quadrilles and they had mazookas and they had waltzes and they had lances and baratas and all that type of music they played those days, you see. Well, they didn't play no jazz, you know what I mean. Now, old Mamanetta, he was a fine, oh, ace trumpet player, but no jazz, you know. Strictly music, strictly music, and so on. And that's what they played, see. But this jazz business, I didn't start to play in that until I got mixed up with punk and the jazz, you know, and playing around them places. And that come in right after bowling, you see. And the Imperial Band, Perez and those fellas, they started playing. Well, that's why jazz came in. And then all those other boys, these white boys, like Sharky and Rennie, well, they come after that. Well, they picked up right from that and just went right along with it, you see.
Who do you think was the first band to ever play any jazz or whatever?

Well, I attribute it to bowling, you know. The simple fact, the way that thing come about, you see, bowling was a fellow, he didn't know the big as his house, you understand what I mean. And whatever they played, they caught or made up, you see. They made their own music, and they played it their own way, you understand. So that's where jazz started, you understand. Just through the feeling of the man, you understand. He's in provision, you see. And then the surroundings, because the surroundings at that time was mostly people of, or you might say, of a fast type, you know, exciting, you understand. And there's old blues and all that stuff, you know, that came in there, you see. And eventually the jazz business started to go on, you see. But the old time musicians, they didn't play nothing but music, you know.

By the way, I'm about to explain to you. We have a paper, you know, that we'll sign and you sign. And you can put any restrictions on it. Yeah. If you want to say anything, you know, and hold it back.
That's detrimental to anybody, you know what I mean.
Yeah, you can hold it back for 10 years or 20 years or. No need to knock anybody.
No, no. But that's facts when I'm, you see, that's authentic. What I'm telling you, I can back that up because.
Yeah, well, that's right.

Now, you take a lot of those fellas, they were routine players. And that's where jazz came from, you understand. That's where jazz came from, from the routine men, you understand. The men that didn't know nothing about music. They just made up their own ideas. They didn't know nothing about phrasing, nothing in music. No thoughts at all about music. Just go ahead and play, that's all, you understand. That's how jazz came about.
And they were mixed up with this fast life, huh?

Oh yeah, those days, man, things was wide open. The New Orleans was, they had hunky-tunks, you know, you understand. All that, all the lowest type of, you understand, would be in those places, you know. Rouse the bouts off the river and all that sort of stuff, you know.
When did you hear Bolden? You say you heard him over here?

I heard him once, yes. I was a kid. I was just fixing to start out, you know, man. I was just fixing to go out and start playing. And he played over here once and I heard him play. Well, like I told you, he died a young man, you know. He wasn't old.
Do you remember about what year that was?
Well, that was around, I might say around 19, six or seven, around here, somewhere around there.
How many were you born? 87. 87.
87, yeah.
So you would have been almost?
Oh, I was around in my teens then, see.
Yeah, 15 or 18.

Now, he was a fine-looking fellow and a healthy-looking fellow, but like, you know, the life, you understand what I mean? This fast life, it broke him all up. So many of them do the same thing, you know.
And you remember how he sounded and how he played?

Oh, yeah, he was powerful, you know. He had plenty of power, you know. He had a good style, you know, and bruised and all that stuff. But as far as anything else, there was nothing to it, you know. And just like all those other boys, I betty was a good man too. Chad Rene was another good man. They had good potentialities, but they never did develop them, you understand? They never did study, you see. They had the lip and everything. They made fine musicians up there to study, but they just went on playing, that's all, see. And made money, you understand? That's all they wanted, see. That's all it was, see.
What about Bolden? Does anybody who's made records or who's around today play anything like him?

Well, I don't know. It's practically, you take certain types now. You take Bolden and, say, Freddie Keppert, now he died in Chicago. They were mostly on the same style. They were powerful trumpet players and they mostly, well, the improvisation is always going to be a little different, you know, and they're no two men alike, you understand? But it's the similarity there, you understand what I mean, between them and the style was just a forceful trumpet player, you understand? Just strong and came out.
How did Joe Oliver compare?

Well, Joe was good too. Joe was very good. I played with him a lot too. Well, Joe was powerful. He didn't have too much of a tone, but he was good for jazz because he could make all that, he could make it go like a dog and all that, you understand? You know, that wah-wah stuff and he'd make all that on the horn, you know? And he was strong, you know, he's a big fella, as big as you, you know? You saw him, huh? No. You ever seen? Same picture, he's a terrible picture. Yeah, he was a very big fella. I got a picture of him there. He's big as Bill, huh? Oh, Lord, yeah, he was a heavy man. He weighed about 200. He's a good big man, this man.
Not as big as me, though.

Not fat like you. But he was all right. Joe was a nice fella, you know? He played quite a bit of trouble. He made quite a hit in Chicago, too. He brought Louie up there, you know? Yeah, he was the one who brought Louie up there.
What about, say, Wooden Joe as compared with Wooden?
Well, that's the difference altogether. He never made to hear what these men made, you know? Joe was mostly local stuff. He never went anywhere in the way of speaking, you know?
I just wondered if he played as loud as Bowden Joe.
Well, they could all play loud. Boy's blasting is concerned. All them guys could play loud. That was just tight, you know? Just hollow blow, that's all. What about fingering?
Did Bowden have fast fingering or any tricks?

Well, it's the style they play, you understand? Yeah. Of course, fingering goes a long way, you know? You take fingering, if you compare a man with fingering, you take a man and play like tico-tico and things like that, well, that's not the question, you understand? Yeah. But playing jazz, you'll notice that the very few of them fellas that played that kind of jazz did any fast stringing. It was mostly an improvisation that was lento and loud, but nothing too fancy, you understand what I mean? It was just a different improvisation altogether. Yeah.
I just wondered how he bent his tone or if he used half elvin.

Boy, he just blowin', man. He had a record for that. I'll tell you what it was. They had a park they called the Johnson Park, you see? Yeah. And then the Laken Park. Well, they was about, oh, about two parks apart, you see. Well, the bowling would be playing at the Johnson Park and the Robeshow Band or some other band that was at Lincoln Park, you see, where bowling hit you to the side of the window there and blow through that window so the people at the Lincoln Park could hear him, you know? They'd all come over by going. That was something, man. Yeah. So you know there was loud blowers, eh? Yeah.
Who was in the band when you heard him?

Did you know any of the guys? Well, I played with some of the men that he had after he died. I'll tell you how that come about. He had the bowling band. Now, he had a fella called Frank Lewis playing clarinet. And he had a rock mumpert on guitar. And he had a fella called Bob Lyons playing bass. And he was on trumpet. And I think it was D.D. Chandler, one of the old drummers was playing with him. And Cornish was playing trombone. That's the first band he had, see?
Do you want to stop and answer the phone?

No, that'll answer the town set. So, later on, a fella by the name of Frankie Dusen, a trombone player, he started playing with him, see? That's just before Bowling died, see? That's before he went and got sick, in other words. Well, after Bowling left out, then Frankie took the band over. This Dusen was a fella, the trombone player, and he called it the Eagle Band, see? Well, I played with the Eagle Band, with Dusen, because he's from over this side of the river, see? And he knew me as a kid, you know? Well, I played with some of the Bowling's old men in that band, see? Because Frankie kept the same fellas, but just him and I was different, you see?
You played the violin? Yeah, the violin.
Yeah, we played it out. We used to play at the old Masonic Hall there, you know, and play Scourge and Trips, and play all these dances and things around the town there, you know?
Who played cornet?

Well, a fella by the name of Edwild Clemmen, at that time. And then, later on, Bunk went with the Eagle Band, too. Now, the funny thing about Bunk, when he was with us downtown, the Superior Band, he didn't drink, he didn't have no bad habits at all. And when he went uptown with the Eagle Band, they ruined him. He started drinking and he went all the pieces, you know? Just ruined himself. It showed you a different environment, you understand? Mm-hmm.
When he was with the Superior, was he a good reader?

Yeah, Bunk, he would read, yes, he could read, sure. We used to play all that old Joplin music, you know? Frog Legs and Cresanum and all that. We had the Red Book, you saw those books. Yeah, sure, I know. Yeah, we used to play all that, yeah. He read well, yeah.
How did Bunk play in those days? I heard him in the late years, but I never knew him before.
Well, he was always a nice soft trumpet player, you know? He never was a blaster, you know? He didn't blast? No, no.
Bold and...

Bunk had a very nice style, you know? He's a... You see, you know, they would play mostly just... All that music was played in a slow tempo, you understand? Mm-hmm. And it looked like he just had the right touch to play that type of music, you understand? It was a slur style, like, you know, like Frog Legs and all those old numbers, Joplin music, you know? And Bunk would look like he was just cut out to play that type of music. Because he could play that vicious type if he wanted to. It was just him, it was just his style was in him to play that way, you know? And we used to play that music to perfection, you know? I mean, yeah, he had it, really had it down.
Would he fake it all? No, no.
Oh, yes, he could fake it all.
No, but I mean on the Joplin numbers.
No, no, yeah, we had the music. We had music for all this stuff, see? Yeah, we had all kinds of music. We used to use plenty of music, you see?
Did you help Bunk much with his reading?
Yes, I helped him some, sure. But he could read when I first met him, you know? Yes, he had some schooling, you understand? He was like the mother fellas. He knew what he was going about, I think.
Some of those Joplin rags are in sharp keys. Yeah, yeah. Did they have to use an A clarinet on those, or what did they do?
No, well, the fellas we had those days, like Louie, he played a C clarinet, see? Oh, yeah. Well, he played off the violin part, see? What kind of a part did he play?
Almost like your violin?

No, he would play, he'd play, he'd get the lead, and then he would make his own improvisions. Variation. Yeah, his variation, his own ideas, you see? But he would, after he'd play it a while, he'd get the melody, you see, and he knew just how to tune what. And that's what he'd been gifted in that type of playing, you know? He knew just what to put in there, see? Now, this Teal, since you spoke about the A clarinet.
Oh, that's the violin?
Yeah, now, he used to take a B clarinet and play the A parts and everything, because he knew the transposition, you see?
Which Teal was this? Lorenzo. Is that the old man or the young one? No, the young fellow.

Well, they were all great, all three of them. His daddy was the clarinet and his uncle was the clarinet player, see? And he was the youngest. Well, he took a B clarinet and he played everything, because he knew the transposition, you see? But he was an ace musician, you see? He went to Chicago and the fellas up there, like Kewley and them fellas, were using the A and B clarinet. And when he sat down and played with that B clarinet, they wondered how he was doing it, you see? Well, he started the transposition, you see? And there's nothing to it if you knew it. Of course, if you don't try to do it well, it's hard, you understand? You take an A clarinet that Papiess wrote in G, you understand? Yeah. He played in two flats, you see? Now, you take a B clarinet and you're playing three shorts, you see? In other words, you put it down a half tone, see?
Yeah.
You see that idea?
Yeah.

But he studied that, you know, and them fellas didn't, I mean, it was depending on two clarinetes, and he'd take one clarinet and do the same work, see? So, you see, it's complicated when you get into music, you understand? I mean, you see a guy blowing in his beat course, jazz is nice and everything, but if you get away from jazz and you go to talking about musicians, then that's another thing, you see? Now, he could play jazz, too. And he could play anything that you put up there in front of him, see?
Did you call him a real Barrel House musician if he wanted to?

No, no, no Barrel House. He had a nice style of playing, and he just played according to his ideas, you see? But he could play like Pius Society and make all those, and he was gifted, he could fake, and he know the chords and everything, see? That's what he takes.
He wouldn't get Gut Bucket, though? Huh?

Well, yeah, what you call Gut Bucket, you understand? It was the tune. The Gut Bucket is the tune you play. It ain't the man, it's the tune, it's the piece you're playing that makes it Gut Bucket, you see? Of course, some guys play Gut Bucket because they can't play otherwise, you see? Now, Johnny Dots was a pretty good clarinet player. In his style, you know, he played well, you see? Now, you might call him Gut Bucket, you see? But a man like Teo, you couldn't call him Gut Bucket because he's a scholar, you understand? You see, that makes a big difference.
Yes.

It's just like anything else. You take a boy or a child that comes up in a bad environment and you hear him speak, and then get another child that's raised in a school or something in a good environment. Well, it's the same as a musician. If a guy comes up playing a horn and he never had no tuition at all, you wouldn't expect him to play like a man that's been taught, you understand? It's a different feeling and everything, you see? Because the man that's polished is bound to be different from the man that's in the rough, you know? Isn't that a fact? Why sure, absolutely. That's all that difference in Gut Bucket is. It's just getting a Gut Bucket man and a Gut Bucket tune and you've got Gut Bucket, you see? But the other man will play the same thing, but it wouldn't be exactly because there's two different men there, you see? There's two different thoughts, two different feelings, you see? One guy can't play bad if he wanted because he liked right, you see? The other guy can't play right because he can't. He don't know what he's doing. He's just blowing, that's all, you see? That's the whole thing in a nutshell right there, you see?
I wonder if you could tell us a little bit about the T.O. family. Lorenzo married your sister.
Yes, I can.
Do they have any relatives living?
Yes, he's got some relatives downtown. His mother just died some time ago. That's right. But he's got some nieces in some downtown.
Are their names T.O.?
No, they're married, you know. He's got a brother that's living as a T.O. but he's not a musician. We'd like to look at him.
We'd like to find him and talk to him. Maybe he would remember about his father and all of you.
Well, I could tell you about the father. If you could, let me wonder. The old man, he's Louis T.O. He was the oldest brother. Well, he studied in Mexico, you see?
Were they Mexicans or just studied?

Well, I wouldn't say they're Mexicans, but they had some Spanish blood in them, you understand what I mean? My grandfather was from France and my grandmother was from Hattie, see? Well, that was the beginning of my family, yeah, see? So we mixed up. But he studied in Mexico, you see? And that's why he was such a great musician. Now, he taught the other brother, see? And the other brother, he's come out great too, because his brother taught him, see? Well, he traveled on the road with all his shows, the Nashville students and all them old times. Is that Louis?
It's Lorenzo.
The old Lorenzo.
Yeah, yeah.
Well, the old man traveled too, but when he got old, he had to cut it out. Yeah. But he was a fine director too and everything. He could do regular symphony.
Louis was the one they called Pa Pa?
No, Pa Pa, yes, that's right. Louis was Pa Pa. Yeah. And he was the oldest boy. Yeah, that's right. Lorenzo is this boy's daddy. He's Lorenzo Junior, see? Mm-hmm.
You want to see his picture? Yes, I'd like to. Not the old man, but I mean the boy.

Yes. Just find a few people. Oh, nice picture. Yeah, that's the band was in New York. These pictures were taken in New York then. Yeah, it was lobbies. We was playing the shows then. The Strand in Y. Mm-hmm. That's in there, see?
Yes. Yes. Yes. That's his son.
Ricard Alexis told me he was raised over in the Bay St. Louis. Bay St. Louis.
Yeah.
Bay St. Louis, over that way. Yeah. And he said that the T.O.s lived over there for a while.
Yeah, they did, yeah.

I didn't know that. I didn't know that. I didn't know that. I'm surprised. Mm-hmm. They didn't come from there though then, you think? No, they went over there for a while, you know. But they're right here from the city.

Yeah. I'm saying, I'm not sure. Yeah. I'm not sure. Yeah. I'm not sure. Yeah. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. But they lived over there for a while. Yeah, they did, yeah. I didn't know that. I'm surprised. Mm-hmm. They didn't come from there though then, you think?
No, they went over there for a while, you know. But they're right here from the city.
So, Warnick didn't play clarinet at the time?

No, he was playing saxophone alto. Only. But he played clarinet. He taught him in other ways. T.O. taught him. Mm-hmm. And who's the sousaphone player? This fellow here. He's in New York now. He's a British subject. A.C. Gary is his name. A.C. Gary? Yeah, this is Johnny Lindsey. He played the trombone.
I knew him.
He died in Chicago. That's Steve Lewis.
And is that your brother?
That's my brother, Charlie. And that's me there, see? Mm-hmm. That's the same band.
Mm-hmm.
Now here's the, here's the crew old Saturdays in the Absinthe House. We stayed two years on WWL with that band.
Now we have a violin player here and a trumpet player.
That's me.
That's you.
That's your both. That's my brother there. He's in California now. He's a sousaphone player.
What is his name? Henry. And that's Warnick? That's Warnick, yeah.
And this? That's Joe Newman, he's playing with bass in our bass. That's his daddy, Dwight Newman. And the drummer?
Henry Martin.

Henry Martin. Mm-hmm. And that's Charlie, my brother there. That's the old Absinthe House. See that rail you've been in there, eh? Mm-hmm. That old rail and everything. We stayed there for three years in that job. They were dancing there then, you know?
Mm-hmm. Who replaced you in the old Absinthe House?
I see you. I think after we left there, they cut the dancing out. I don't remember. And who was there before you? I think the melon pickers played in there a while. Oh, yeah.
Who was there before you? Do you remember?
Well, it was the Jitney dance before we went in there.
Oh, I thought maybe that was when the original Dixieland Jazz Band came in. No, no. No, that's a nice picture.
That's, uh, Mr. Russell gave it in. Mm-hmm.
Oh, I see. And it says leader on your cap. What does that mean? Well, I was a leader. Yeah, but I mean, I'm trying to get at what's the difference between leader and manager?
Oh, the manager was a fellow. He took care of the job, you know. The business part. Yeah, the business part.
He collected the money, huh?
Mm-hmm. I run the band when he's on the stands. Well, who picked the-
Did you stop off? How did you start the band? You started playing?
That's the way we did those. The violin player always did that. Yeah, always stop and start the band. And I selected whatever the band had to play. Yeah, right.
And none of the others have anything on the cap but Superior Hall.
That's right. That's the band. Oh, I see. How old do you think I was there?
Let's see, that would be 1910 or so. Then you were born in 1887. 23?
No, about 21 when that thing.
21. 21. So that would be-
It looked like a kid, but- 1908, maybe along in there. Yeah, 1989. Gee, that clarinet looks funny, doesn't it? Yeah, that's a shoe clarinet, see? Yeah, that's a shoe clarinet, see?
Yeah. Now this is Marrera, yeah.

That's John Marrera's daddy. Lawrence Marrera. Yeah, we know Lawrence. Yeah, that's his daddy. How come they call him Moran? I never could figure that out, could you? Billy Moran, they say Moran because they couldn't say Marrera, you know?
Some say Moran, but Billy Morera was his name, see? Yeah.
Now here's a- Show you.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
or marimba or what? I used to play that. That's what I wanted to ask you about. When you played that?
Well that's not a song.
